items.title: I can explain why carbon forms four covalent bonds using its valence electron configuration
items.what: Carbon is in group 14 and has four valence electrons in its outer shell. To achieve stability it shares all four electrons, forming four covalent bonds with neighbouring non-metallic atoms.
items.why: This explains why carbon can bond to so many different atoms and to other carbon atoms in chains and rings, creating the enormous structural diversity seen in organic chemistry.
items.example: In methane (CH4), carbon shares one electron with each of four hydrogen atoms, giving carbon a full outer shell of eight electrons.

subtopic.name: Carbon Bonding and Structural Diversity
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines why carbon forms such a wide variety of stable compounds, focusing on its four valence electrons, the strength and stability of different covalent bonds it forms, and how structural isomers arise. It also introduces the concept of degree of unsaturation.
subtopic.why: Understanding why carbon is central to organic chemistry allows you to predict the range of structures a molecule can adopt and compare the stability of different bonds, which is foundational for all subsequent work in organic chemistry.

items.title: I can define bond strength and compare the relative strengths of common covalent bonds in organic molecules
items.what: Bond strength (average bond energy) is the energy in kJ mol⁻¹ required to break one mole of a specific covalent bond in the gaseous state. Higher bond energy means a stronger and more stable bond.
items.why: Comparing bond strengths helps predict which bonds in a molecule are most likely to break during a chemical reaction, and why some molecules are more chemically stable than others.
items.example: A C–F bond (485 kJ mol⁻¹) is stronger and more stable than a C–I bond (240 kJ mol⁻¹) because fluorine has a smaller atomic radius, resulting in a shorter, stronger bond.

subtopic.why: Understanding why carbon is central to organic chemistry allows you to predict the range of structures a molecule can adopt and compare the stability of different bonds, which is foundational for all subsequent work in organic chemistry.

items.title: I can explain the two key trends in average bond energy for carbon bonds
items.what: Bond energy increases as the number of bonds between two atoms increases (C–C < C=C < C≡C). Bond energy decreases as you move down a group in the periodic table for bonds to carbon (C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I).
items.why: These trends allow you to rank bond stability without memorising every individual value, and to explain why longer bonds (formed with larger atoms) are generally weaker and less stable.
items.example: A C=C double bond has a bond energy of 614 kJ mol⁻¹ compared to 347 kJ mol⁻¹ for a C–C single bond, so the double bond requires more energy to break.

items.title: I can identify and distinguish between the three types of structural isomers
items.what: Structural isomers share the same molecular formula but differ in how their atoms are connected. The three types are skeletal isomers (different carbon frameworks), positional isomers (same functional group in different positions) and functional group isomers (different types of functional group).
items.why: Recognising isomerism explains why two compounds with identical molecular formulas can have very different physical and chemical properties, which is important for synthesis and identification work.
items.example: Pentan-1-ol, pentan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol all have the molecular formula C5H12O but differ in the position of the –OH group, making them positional isomers of each other.

subtopic.why: Understanding why carbon is central to organic chemistry allows you to predict the range of structures a molecule can adopt and compare the stability of different bonds, which is foundational for all subsequent work in organic chemistry.

items.title: I can calculate degree of unsaturation from a molecular formula
items.what: Degree of unsaturation (DoU) is calculated using the formula DoU = (2C + 2 + N – H – X) / 2, where C is carbon count, N is nitrogen count, H is hydrogen count and X is halogen count. Each double bond or ring contributes 1 to the DoU.
items.why: Calculating the DoU from a molecular formula lets you quickly determine how many double bonds or rings a molecule contains before you see its structure, which helps with identifying unknown compounds.
items.example: For benzene C6H6: DoU = (2×6 + 2 – 6) / 2 = 4, which accounts for the three double bonds and one ring in its structure.

subtopic.name: Carbon Bonding and Structural Diversity
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines why carbon forms such a wide variety of stable compounds, focusing on its four valence electrons, the strength and stability of different covalent bonds it forms, and how structural isomers arise. It also introduces the concept of degree of unsaturation.
subtopic.why: Understanding why carbon is central to organic chemistry allows you to predict the range of structures a molecule can adopt and compare the stability of different bonds, which is foundational for all subsequent work in organic chemistry.

items.title: I can determine degree of unsaturation by counting double bonds and rings in a structural formula
items.what: When a structure is known, the DoU equals the total number of double bonds (including C=O) plus the number of ring systems present in the molecule.
items.why: This approach acts as a cross-check when both the structure and molecular formula are available, confirming that the structure and formula are consistent with each other.
items.example: A molecule containing one C=C double bond, one C=O group and one cyclic ring has a DoU of 3.

subtopic.name: Carbon Bonding and Structural Diversity
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines why carbon forms such a wide variety of stable compounds, focusing on its four valence electrons, the strength and stability of different covalent bonds it forms, and how structural isomers arise. It also introduces the concept of degree of unsaturation.
subtopic.why: Understanding why carbon is central to organic chemistry allows you to predict the range of structures a molecule can adopt and compare the stability of different bonds, which is foundational for all subsequent work in organic chemistry.

items.title: I can write the molecular formula of an organic compound from its structure
items.what: The molecular formula lists each element present and the total number of atoms of that element using subscript numbers, with carbon listed first, then hydrogen, then all other elements alphabetically.
items.why: The molecular formula gives the simplest summary of a compound's composition and is needed for calculating molar mass, degree of unsaturation and identifying possible isomers.
items.example: The molecular formula of ethanol is C2H6O, indicating 2 carbon atoms, 6 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

subtopic.name: Representing Organic Molecules
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the four main ways to represent organic molecules: molecular formula, structural formula, semi-structural (condensed) formula and skeletal formula. It explains the conventions for each representation and when each is most appropriate.
subtopic.why: Being able to read and draw molecules in multiple representations is a core practical skill in organic chemistry, as different contexts and audiences require different levels of structural detail.

items.title: I can draw and interpret the structural formula of an organic molecule
items.what: The structural formula shows every atom by its chemical symbol with lines representing each individual bond (one line for a single bond, two lines for a double bond). Every hydrogen atom is explicitly shown.
items.why: The structural formula makes all bonding connections visible, which is essential when learning to identify functional groups and understand how atoms are arranged in a molecule.
items.example: In the structural formula of propan-1-ol, the three carbon atoms are shown in a chain with all hydrogen atoms drawn individually and the –OH group clearly visible on the first carbon.

subtopic.name: Representing Organic Molecules
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the four main ways to represent organic molecules: molecular formula, structural formula, semi-structural (condensed) formula and skeletal formula. It explains the conventions for each representation and when each is most appropriate.
subtopic.why: Being able to read and draw molecules in multiple representations is a core practical skill in organic chemistry, as different contexts and audiences require different levels of structural detail.

items.title: I can write and interpret the semi-structural (condensed) formula of an organic molecule
items.what: The semi-structural formula groups hydrogen atoms with their carbon (e.g. CH3, CH2) and omits most bond lines. Brackets are used to indicate repeating units and branching alkyl groups.
items.why: Semi-structural formulas are more compact than full structural formulas and are widely used in written communication, making them important for answering exam questions and reading scientific texts.
items.example: Hexane written as a semi-structural formula is CH3(CH2)4CH3, where the four repeating CH2 groups are condensed into brackets with a subscript.

subtopic.name: Representing Organic Molecules
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the four main ways to represent organic molecules: molecular formula, structural formula, semi-structural (condensed) formula and skeletal formula. It explains the conventions for each representation and when each is most appropriate.
subtopic.why: Being able to read and draw molecules in multiple representations is a core practical skill in organic chemistry, as different contexts and audiences require different levels of structural detail.

items.title: I can draw and interpret the skeletal formula of an organic molecule
items.what: In a skeletal formula, the carbon chain is shown as a zigzag line where each vertex and end represents a carbon atom. Hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon are not shown; all other atoms and any hydrogen bonded to non-carbon atoms are explicitly labelled.
items.why: Skeletal formulas are the standard representation used in higher-level chemistry because they are quick to draw, space-efficient and make functional groups stand out clearly.
items.example: Butan-1-ol is drawn as a four-carbon zigzag line with –OH written at the leftmost carbon. The carbon atoms and their attached hydrogens are understood but not drawn.

subtopic.name: Representing Organic Molecules
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the four main ways to represent organic molecules: molecular formula, structural formula, semi-structural (condensed) formula and skeletal formula. It explains the conventions for each representation and when each is most appropriate.
subtopic.why: Being able to read and draw molecules in multiple representations is a core practical skill in organic chemistry, as different contexts and audiences require different levels of structural detail.

items.title: I can determine the number of hydrogen atoms on each carbon in a skeletal formula
items.what: Every carbon in a skeletal formula must have exactly four bonds. The number of implied hydrogen atoms on any carbon equals four minus the number of visible bonds drawn to that carbon.
items.why: This skill is needed to convert between skeletal and other formula types, and to check that a drawn structure is chemically valid with no carbon having fewer or more than four bonds.
items.example: A carbon at the end of a skeletal chain has one visible bond to the adjacent carbon, so it has three implied hydrogen atoms (4 – 1 = 3), representing a –CH3 group.

subtopic.name: Representing Organic Molecules
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the four main ways to represent organic molecules: molecular formula, structural formula, semi-structural (condensed) formula and skeletal formula. It explains the conventions for each representation and when each is most appropriate.
subtopic.why: Being able to read and draw molecules in multiple representations is a core practical skill in organic chemistry, as different contexts and audiences require different levels of structural detail.

items.title: I can convert between molecular, structural, semi-structural and skeletal representations of an organic molecule
items.what: Converting between representations requires identifying the parent carbon chain, locating functional groups and applying the conventions specific to the target representation.
items.why: Exam questions routinely require drawing or naming compounds from any starting representation, so fluency in conversion is essential for demonstrating full understanding.
items.example: Given the semi-structural formula CH3CHBrCH2CH3, you identify the 4-carbon parent chain, place the bromo group on carbon 2 and draw the corresponding skeletal formula as a four-carbon zigzag with Br attached at the second vertex.

subtopic.name: Representing Organic Molecules
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the four main ways to represent organic molecules: molecular formula, structural formula, semi-structural (condensed) formula and skeletal formula. It explains the conventions for each representation and when each is most appropriate.
subtopic.why: Being able to read and draw molecules in multiple representations is a core practical skill in organic chemistry, as different contexts and audiences require different levels of structural detail.

items.title: I can describe the features of a homologous series and give examples
items.what: A homologous series is a sequence of compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, where each member differs from the next by one –CH2– unit. All members share the same general formula.
items.why: Understanding homologous series lets you predict the properties of unfamiliar molecules by comparing them to known members of the same family, without needing to study each compound individually.
items.example: The alkane series (methane, ethane, propane, butane…) all have only C–C single bonds and follow the general formula CnH2n+2, with each member having one more CH2 than the previous.

subtopic.name: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Cyclic Compounds
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, homologous series and systematic IUPAC naming of alkanes (including branched isomers), alkenes, cyclohexane and benzene. It also introduces the concept of a homologous series and saturated versus unsaturated molecules.
subtopic.why: Hydrocarbons form the backbone of all organic molecules. Mastering their naming rules provides the foundation for naming every other functional group family, since all organic compound names are built on the parent hydrocarbon chain.

items.title: I can name straight-chain and branched alkanes using IUPAC rules up to C8
items.what: Alkane names are based on the longest continuous carbon chain (parent hydrocarbon), ending in '-ane'. Alkyl branches are named as prefixes with their position number, and the chain is numbered from the end that gives the lowest locants to substituents.
items.why: Systematic naming ensures that every molecule has exactly one correct name and that any trained chemist can draw the structure from the name alone, enabling unambiguous communication.
items.example: The alkane with a 6-carbon chain and a methyl group on the third carbon is named 3-methylhexane, not 4-methylhexane, because the end closest to the branch is used for numbering.

subtopic.name: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Cyclic Compounds
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, homologous series and systematic IUPAC naming of alkanes (including branched isomers), alkenes, cyclohexane and benzene. It also introduces the concept of a homologous series and saturated versus unsaturated molecules.
subtopic.why: Hydrocarbons form the backbone of all organic molecules. Mastering their naming rules provides the foundation for naming every other functional group family, since all organic compound names are built on the parent hydrocarbon chain.

items.title: I can draw the structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas of alkanes from their IUPAC names
items.what: Working from a name, identify the parent chain length, draw the carbon skeleton, add any alkyl branches at their stated positions, and fill in all hydrogen atoms to satisfy four bonds per carbon.
items.why: Drawing structures from names is the reverse of naming and is equally tested in exams; it confirms that you understand what each part of a name represents structurally.
items.example: 2,4-dimethylhexane has a 6-carbon parent chain with methyl groups on carbons 2 and 4. The skeletal formula is a 6-carbon zigzag with single-carbon branches at the second and fourth vertices.

subtopic.name: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Cyclic Compounds
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, homologous series and systematic IUPAC naming of alkanes (including branched isomers), alkenes, cyclohexane and benzene. It also introduces the concept of a homologous series and saturated versus unsaturated molecules.
subtopic.why: Hydrocarbons form the backbone of all organic molecules. Mastering their naming rules provides the foundation for naming every other functional group family, since all organic compound names are built on the parent hydrocarbon chain.

items.title: I can name straight-chain and branched alkenes using IUPAC rules, specifying the position of the double bond
items.what: Alkene names end in '-ene' and include a number indicating the first carbon of the C=C double bond. The chain is numbered from the end closest to the double bond to give it the lowest possible locant.
items.why: Because positional isomers of alkenes are possible for chains of four or more carbons, specifying the double bond position is essential to identify the correct compound.
items.example: CH2=CHCH2CH3 is named but-1-ene, not but-3-ene, because the double bond begins at carbon 1 when the chain is numbered from the end closest to it.

subtopic.name: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Cyclic Compounds
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, homologous series and systematic IUPAC naming of alkanes (including branched isomers), alkenes, cyclohexane and benzene. It also introduces the concept of a homologous series and saturated versus unsaturated molecules.
subtopic.why: Hydrocarbons form the backbone of all organic molecules. Mastering their naming rules provides the foundation for naming every other functional group family, since all organic compound names are built on the parent hydrocarbon chain.

items.title: I can draw the structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas of alkenes from their IUPAC names
items.what: Drawing an alkene from its name requires placing the C=C double bond at the specified carbon position and ensuring the double bond carbon atoms each have the correct number of remaining bonds to hydrogen or other groups.
items.why: Drawing alkenes accurately, including the correct position and geometry of the double bond, is required for answering naming and structure questions in assessments.
items.example: 2-methylpent-2-ene has a 5-carbon chain with a double bond starting at carbon 2 and a methyl branch also at carbon 2. The skeletal formula shows a double bond between the second and third vertices with a branch at the second vertex.

subtopic.name: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Cyclic Compounds
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, homologous series and systematic IUPAC naming of alkanes (including branched isomers), alkenes, cyclohexane and benzene. It also introduces the concept of a homologous series and saturated versus unsaturated molecules.
subtopic.why: Hydrocarbons form the backbone of all organic molecules. Mastering their naming rules provides the foundation for naming every other functional group family, since all organic compound names are built on the parent hydrocarbon chain.

items.title: I can describe the structure of cyclohexane and represent it using a skeletal formula
items.what: Cyclohexane (C6H12) is a saturated cyclic alkane in which six carbon atoms are connected in a ring, each bonded to two hydrogen atoms. Its skeletal formula is drawn as a regular hexagon with no double bonds.
items.why: Cyclohexane is a commonly encountered ring structure in chemistry and biochemistry, and understanding cyclic structures extends the naming and structural rules learned for straight-chain alkanes.
items.example: The skeletal formula of cyclohexane is a plain hexagon. Each vertex represents a CH2 group, and the molecular formula C6H12 confirms it is saturated despite not fitting the CnH2n+2 formula of open-chain alkanes.

subtopic.name: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Cyclic Compounds
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, homologous series and systematic IUPAC naming of alkanes (including branched isomers), alkenes, cyclohexane and benzene. It also introduces the concept of a homologous series and saturated versus unsaturated molecules.
subtopic.why: Hydrocarbons form the backbone of all organic molecules. Mastering their naming rules provides the foundation for naming every other functional group family, since all organic compound names are built on the parent hydrocarbon chain.

items.title: I can describe the structure of benzene and explain why it is represented with a circle inside a hexagon
items.what: Benzene (C6H6) is a planar cyclic molecule in which each carbon contributes one electron to a ring of delocalised electrons above and below the plane. This is represented as a hexagon with a circle inside, or alternatively with three alternating double bonds.
items.why: The delocalised electron ring gives benzene greater stability than a typical alkene. Recognising benzene's unique structure is necessary for understanding its physical properties and later reaction chemistry.
items.example: Because benzene has a ring of delocalised electrons rather than fixed double bonds, it does not readily undergo addition reactions the way alkenes do, making it more chemically stable.

subtopic.name: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Cyclic Compounds
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, homologous series and systematic IUPAC naming of alkanes (including branched isomers), alkenes, cyclohexane and benzene. It also introduces the concept of a homologous series and saturated versus unsaturated molecules.
subtopic.why: Hydrocarbons form the backbone of all organic molecules. Mastering their naming rules provides the foundation for naming every other functional group family, since all organic compound names are built on the parent hydrocarbon chain.

items.title: I can name haloalkanes using IUPAC rules, specifying the halogen type and its position on the chain
items.what: Haloalkane names use the prefixes fluoro-, chloro-, bromo- or iodo- before the parent alkane name. The chain is numbered from the end closest to the halogen to give it the lowest locant, and di-, tri-, tetra- prefixes are used for multiple identical halogens.
items.why: Haloalkanes are used as refrigerants, solvents and in pharmaceutical synthesis. Correct naming is needed to communicate precise structural information about which carbon bears the halogen.
items.example: CH3CHClCH2CH3 is named 2-chlorobutane because the chlorine is on the second carbon of a 4-carbon chain, and the chain is numbered from the end closest to the chlorine.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Haloalkanes, Amines and Alcohols
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, IUPAC naming and classification of haloalkanes (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-), primary amines and alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary), including drawing all three types of formula representations.
subtopic.why: These three functional group families appear widely in pharmaceuticals, industrial solvents and biological molecules. Knowing how to identify, name and classify them is essential for the organic reactions topics that follow.

items.title: I can draw the structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas of haloalkanes from their IUPAC names
items.what: Working from a haloalkane name, draw the parent carbon chain, attach the halogen symbol at the stated carbon position and complete the hydrogen count so each carbon has four bonds.
items.why: Drawing haloalkanes accurately from names is tested directly in exams and is needed before studying nucleophilic substitution reactions in later units.
items.example: 2-fluoro-3-methylpentane has a 5-carbon parent chain with F on carbon 2 and a methyl branch on carbon 3. In the skeletal formula, F is drawn at the second vertex and a one-carbon branch at the third.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Haloalkanes, Amines and Alcohols
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, IUPAC naming and classification of haloalkanes (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-), primary amines and alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary), including drawing all three types of formula representations.
subtopic.why: These three functional group families appear widely in pharmaceuticals, industrial solvents and biological molecules. Knowing how to identify, name and classify them is essential for the organic reactions topics that follow.

items.title: I can distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols based on their carbon structure
items.what: The classification depends on how many alkyl groups (R groups) are bonded to the carbon bearing the –OH group. One alkyl group (or none) gives a primary alcohol, two gives secondary and three gives tertiary.
items.why: The type of alcohol affects how it reacts in oxidation reactions, which is a major topic in Unit 4. Correctly classifying an alcohol is therefore needed for predicting its reaction products.
items.example: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol because its central carbon carries the –OH group and is bonded to two other carbon-containing groups (two CH3 groups).

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Haloalkanes, Amines and Alcohols
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, IUPAC naming and classification of haloalkanes (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-), primary amines and alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary), including drawing all three types of formula representations.
subtopic.why: These three functional group families appear widely in pharmaceuticals, industrial solvents and biological molecules. Knowing how to identify, name and classify them is essential for the organic reactions topics that follow.

items.title: I can name primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols using IUPAC rules up to C8
items.what: Alcohol names are formed by replacing the terminal '-e' of the parent alkane name with '-ol'. The position of the –OH group is stated as a number before '-ol', and the chain is numbered from the end closest to the –OH group.
items.why: Precise naming of alcohols is required to distinguish between isomers with different properties and reactivities, and forms the basis for naming esters and other derivatives.
items.example: An alcohol with a 7-carbon chain, a methyl group on carbon 6 and the –OH on carbon 3 (numbered from the –OH end) is named 6-methylheptan-3-ol.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Haloalkanes, Amines and Alcohols
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, IUPAC naming and classification of haloalkanes (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-), primary amines and alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary), including drawing all three types of formula representations.
subtopic.why: These three functional group families appear widely in pharmaceuticals, industrial solvents and biological molecules. Knowing how to identify, name and classify them is essential for the organic reactions topics that follow.

items.title: I can draw the structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas of alcohols from their IUPAC names
items.what: Working from an alcohol name, draw the parent chain, place the –OH at the stated position and add any alkyl branches, remembering to show the O–H hydrogen in skeletal formulas since it is bonded to a non-carbon atom.
items.why: Drawing correct alcohol structures is an assessed skill and is needed for understanding intermolecular forces and boiling point trends discussed in the physical properties section.
items.example: 2,5-dimethylhexan-1-ol has a 6-carbon parent chain with –OH at carbon 1 and methyl branches at carbons 2 and 5. The skeletal formula shows –OH at the end vertex with branches at the second and fifth vertices.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Haloalkanes, Amines and Alcohols
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, IUPAC naming and classification of haloalkanes (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-), primary amines and alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary), including drawing all three types of formula representations.
subtopic.why: These three functional group families appear widely in pharmaceuticals, industrial solvents and biological molecules. Knowing how to identify, name and classify them is essential for the organic reactions topics that follow.

items.title: I can name primary amines using IUPAC rules and draw their structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas
items.what: Primary amine names replace the terminal '-e' of the parent alkane name with '-amine'. The position of the –NH2 group is stated before '-amine', and the chain is numbered from the end closest to the amino group.
items.why: Amines are the basis of amino acids and many pharmaceuticals, and their naming follows the same logic as alcohols, reinforcing the systematic approach to IUPAC nomenclature.
items.example: 4,4-dimethylpentan-2-amine has a 5-carbon parent chain with –NH2 on carbon 2 and two methyl groups on carbon 4. The skeletal formula shows NH2 at the second vertex and two branches at the fourth.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Haloalkanes, Amines and Alcohols
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structural features, IUPAC naming and classification of haloalkanes (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-), primary amines and alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary), including drawing all three types of formula representations.
subtopic.why: These three functional group families appear widely in pharmaceuticals, industrial solvents and biological molecules. Knowing how to identify, name and classify them is essential for the organic reactions topics that follow.

items.title: I can distinguish between aldehydes and ketones based on the position of the carbonyl group
items.what: In an aldehyde, the carbonyl carbon is at the end of the carbon chain and is bonded to at least one hydrogen atom (–CHO). In a ketone, the carbonyl carbon is within the chain and bonded to two other carbon atoms on either side.
items.why: Aldehydes and ketones have different reactivity in redox reactions (e.g. only aldehydes are oxidised easily), so correctly distinguishing them is essential for predicting reaction outcomes.
items.example: Propanal (CH3CH2CHO) is an aldehyde because the C=O is at carbon 1, whereas propanone (CH3COCH3) is a ketone because the C=O is at carbon 2, between two methyl groups.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids, Esters and Amides
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the carbonyl group (C=O) as it appears in five organic families: aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and primary amides. It covers structural features, IUPAC naming of each family and naming compounds with two functional groups.
subtopic.why: Carbonyl-containing compounds are central to biochemistry, food science and industrial chemistry. These families are also the reactants and products in the condensation and hydrolysis reactions studied in subsequent topics.

items.title: I can name aldehydes and ketones using IUPAC rules and draw their structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas
items.what: Aldehyde names replace the terminal '-e' of the alkane with '-al'; the carbonyl carbon is always carbon 1 by convention so no position number is needed. Ketone names replace '-e' with '-one' and include the position of the carbonyl when isomers are possible.
items.why: Systematic naming of aldehydes and ketones is directly assessed and is needed for later work on organic reactions including reduction, oxidation and condensation.
items.example: 5-methylhexanal has a 6-carbon chain with the aldehyde group at carbon 1 and a methyl branch at carbon 5. Butan-2-one has a 4-carbon chain with the carbonyl at carbon 2.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids, Esters and Amides
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the carbonyl group (C=O) as it appears in five organic families: aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and primary amides. It covers structural features, IUPAC naming of each family and naming compounds with two functional groups.
subtopic.why: Carbonyl-containing compounds are central to biochemistry, food science and industrial chemistry. These families are also the reactants and products in the condensation and hydrolysis reactions studied in subsequent topics.

items.title: I can identify the carboxyl group and name carboxylic acids using IUPAC rules up to C8
items.what: The carboxyl group (–COOH) consists of a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl group. Carboxylic acid names are formed by replacing the terminal '-e' of the alkane with '-oic acid'. The carboxyl carbon is always carbon 1 and no position number is stated.
items.why: Carboxylic acids are the starting material for making esters and amides, and their acidic properties are important in biochemistry. Correct naming is needed before studying condensation reactions.
items.example: 3,4-dimethylpentanoic acid has a 5-carbon parent chain with the carboxyl group at carbon 1 and methyl groups at carbons 3 and 4.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids, Esters and Amides
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the carbonyl group (C=O) as it appears in five organic families: aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and primary amides. It covers structural features, IUPAC naming of each family and naming compounds with two functional groups.
subtopic.why: Carbonyl-containing compounds are central to biochemistry, food science and industrial chemistry. These families are also the reactants and products in the condensation and hydrolysis reactions studied in subsequent topics.

items.title: I can name non-branched esters using IUPAC rules and draw their structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas
items.what: Ester names consist of two words: the alcohol-derived alkyl group first (ending in '-yl') followed by the carboxylic acid-derived part (ending in '-oate'). The carbon count of the alcohol part and acid part are named separately.
items.why: Esters are responsible for many fruit aromas and are used as flavourings and solvents. Naming them correctly also reinforces understanding of how esters are formed from carboxylic acids and alcohols.
items.example: Butyl propanoate has a 3-carbon acid part (propanoate) and a 4-carbon alcohol part (butyl). The ester linkage –COO– connects these two sections.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids, Esters and Amides
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the carbonyl group (C=O) as it appears in five organic families: aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and primary amides. It covers structural features, IUPAC naming of each family and naming compounds with two functional groups.
subtopic.why: Carbonyl-containing compounds are central to biochemistry, food science and industrial chemistry. These families are also the reactants and products in the condensation and hydrolysis reactions studied in subsequent topics.

items.title: I can draw the structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas of primary amides from their IUPAC names
items.what: Primary amides have the general structure RCONH2, where the amide functional group (–CONH2) replaces the –OH of a carboxylic acid. Amide names are formed by replacing '-oic acid' with '-amide'.
items.why: Primary amides are the functional group found at the peptide bond junction in proteins, making them biologically significant. Drawing amide structures accurately is assessed in both naming and structure questions.
items.example: Propanamide (CH3CH2CONH2) has a 3-carbon chain with the –CONH2 group at carbon 1. In the skeletal formula, the NH2 group is shown explicitly since its hydrogens are bonded to nitrogen, not carbon.

items.title: I can name organic compounds containing two identical functional groups
items.what: When two identical functional groups are present, the prefix 'di' is added before the relevant suffix, and the positions of both groups are specified. For hydroxyl groups the suffix becomes '-diol', for aldehyde groups it becomes '-dial', and so on.
items.why: Many biologically important molecules such as amino acids and dicarboxylic acids contain two functional groups, so naming them correctly is essential for work in biochemistry and synthesis.
items.example: Propane-1,3-diol has hydroxyl groups on carbons 1 and 3. Butanedioic acid (succinic acid) has carboxyl groups on each end of a 4-carbon chain.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups: Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids, Esters and Amides

items.title: I can name organic compounds containing two different functional groups using IUPAC priority rules
items.what: When two different functional groups are present, the higher-priority group determines the suffix and the direction of numbering. The priority order (highest first) is: carboxylic acid > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene > haloalkane. The lower-priority group is named as a prefix using its alternative name.
items.why: Having a clear priority hierarchy ensures that every compound with multiple functional groups has one unambiguous name, which is essential for communicating complex organic structures precisely.
items.example: In a molecule with both a ketone (C=O, priority) and a hydroxyl (–OH) group, the ketone determines the suffix '-one', the chain is numbered from the end closest to the ketone, and the hydroxyl group is named 'hydroxy-' as a prefix, giving a name like 4-hydroxypentan-2-one.

items.title: I can identify the types of intermolecular forces present in different families of organic compounds
items.what: All organic molecules experience dispersion forces. Polar molecules with no O–H or N–H bonds (such as haloalkanes, aldehydes, ketones and esters) also experience dipole–dipole interactions. Molecules with O–H or N–H bonds (alcohols, carboxylic acids, primary amines, primary amides) can also form hydrogen bonds.
items.why: The type of intermolecular force present is the starting point for every boiling point, melting point or viscosity comparison question. Getting this step right determines whether the rest of your reasoning is correct.
items.example: Propanone has dispersion forces and dipole–dipole interactions but no hydrogen bonding between propanone molecules (no O–H or N–H bonds), whereas propan-1-ol has dispersion forces and hydrogen bonding through its –OH group.

subtopic.name: Physical Properties of Organic Compounds
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how the type and strength of intermolecular forces in organic molecules determines their boiling point, melting point and viscosity. It covers trends within and between homologous series, including the effects of molar mass and branching.
subtopic.why: Physical property trends underpin practical decisions in chemistry such as selecting solvents, designing fuels and purifying compounds by distillation. Understanding the molecular basis of these trends is also a major source of exam questions.

items.title: I can explain why boiling point increases with molar mass within a homologous series
items.what: As molar mass increases within a homologous series, molecules become larger and have more electrons, which increases the strength of dispersion forces between molecules. More energy is therefore needed to separate molecules into the gas phase, raising the boiling point.
items.why: This trend is the most commonly tested in exam questions and applies to every homologous series covered in the course, so the underlying reasoning must be expressed clearly and precisely.
items.example: Hexan-1-ol (C6H13OH, bp 157°C) has a higher boiling point than butan-1-ol (C4H9OH, bp 117°C) because the larger molecule has stronger dispersion forces between its molecules.

subtopic.name: Physical Properties of Organic Compounds
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how the type and strength of intermolecular forces in organic molecules determines their boiling point, melting point and viscosity. It covers trends within and between homologous series, including the effects of molar mass and branching.
subtopic.why: Physical property trends underpin practical decisions in chemistry such as selecting solvents, designing fuels and purifying compounds by distillation. Understanding the molecular basis of these trends is also a major source of exam questions.

items.title: I can explain why boiling point decreases as the number of alkyl branches increases among structural isomers
items.what: Branched isomers adopt a more compact, rounded shape compared to straight-chain isomers. This reduces the surface area of contact between neighbouring molecules, weakening dispersion forces and lowering the boiling point.
items.why: This trend applies to all homologous series and is commonly tested alongside the molar mass trend. Understanding both effects allows you to rank isomers by boiling point.
items.example: Pentane (bp 36°C) has a higher boiling point than 2-methylbutane (bp 28°C) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (bp 9°C) even though all three have the molecular formula C5H12, because increased branching reduces intermolecular surface contact.

items.title: I can compare the boiling points of compounds from different homologous series with similar molar masses
items.what: When comparing compounds of similar molar mass from different families, those capable of hydrogen bonding have the highest boiling points, followed by those with dipole–dipole interactions, and finally those with only dispersion forces.
items.why: Cross-family comparisons appear in exam questions and require you to apply knowledge of both intermolecular force type and molar mass simultaneously to rank compounds correctly.
items.example: Among pentane (dispersion only), butan-2-one (dipole–dipole) and butan-1-ol (hydrogen bonding), all with similar molar masses around 72–74 g mol⁻¹, the boiling point order is pentane < butan-2-one < butan-1-ol.

items.title: I can explain trends in melting point within a homologous series using intermolecular forces
items.what: Melting point trends follow the same logic as boiling point trends: larger molecules in a homologous series have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to break the ordered solid structure and melt the substance.
items.why: Melting point data is used to identify compounds and assess purity. Explaining melting point trends using intermolecular force reasoning demonstrates the same core understanding as for boiling points.
items.example: In the n-alkane series, octane (C8H18) has a higher melting point than propane (C3H8) because octane molecules are larger, creating stronger dispersion forces that hold the solid lattice together more firmly.

items.title: I can explain what viscosity is and describe how it changes with molar mass and with temperature
items.what: Viscosity is a measure of a fluid's resistance to flow, arising from intermolecular forces between molecules. Viscosity increases with molar mass within a homologous series (stronger intermolecular forces resist flow) and decreases as temperature increases (greater kinetic energy overcomes intermolecular forces).
items.why: Viscosity is a practically important property in areas such as fuel design, lubrication and food science. Understanding its molecular basis connects intermolecular force theory to real-world applications.
items.example: Octane (molar mass 114 g mol⁻¹, viscosity 0.509 mPa·s) is more viscous than pentane (molar mass 72 g mol⁻¹, viscosity 0.224 mPa·s) at 20°C because its larger molecules form stronger dispersion forces that resist flow.
